lesson_title: The Three Highs That Run South Africa's Weather
hook_text: 34 degrees in Durban. In July. Here's the hairdryer wind your textbook calls a berg wind.
clip_script: In winter, the heavy inside guard piles air up on the plateau, a kilometre and a half above the sea. When a passing weather system tugs at the coast, that plateau air spills over the edge of the escarpment and falls toward the sea. Falling air gets squashed, and squashed air heats up — about one degree warmer for every hundred metres it drops. By the time it reaches Durban it has fallen well over a kilometre and warmed by more than ten degrees: a hot, utterly dry, gusty wind blowing from the land out to sea. It is a hairdryer pointed at the coast — and it is the fire wind.
visual_style: Cross-section animation: air sliding off the plateau, down the escarpment, a thermometer climbing one degree per hundred metres of descent, ending on a sweltering beachfront with fire-danger flags snapping in the wind.
pacing: Hook on the impossible temperature, steady build down the escarpment, hot punchy landing.
